title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
AI systems were used to create a fabricated interview between a Reserve Bank governor and a finance presenter to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The deepfake content was deployed at scale on hosting platforms without human verification before or after publication. This is an impersonation attack, where AI generated false statements attributed to real people in order to deceive potential investors.

The system succeeded because it reached people who did not verify the interview's authenticity or check whether the promoted platform held proper regulatory licenses. Catching this would have required either the platforms hosting the content to review it before publication, or readers to cross-check claims against official regulatory records. It is not established whether the platforms knew the content was fraudulent when they published it.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fabricated article featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler has become the latest example of AI-generated investment scams. The fake article promoted Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform, which authorities warn against. The interview never occurred, and this type of deception is increasingly common as scammers use artificial intelligence to create convincing deepfakes and fake celebrity endorsements.

According to research from the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, investment scams using fabricated content have surged dramatically. Last year, regulators removed 19,400 scams overall, a 182 percent increase, including 5,476 phishing scams and 7,051 fake investment platforms. Notable Australians frequently impersonated include Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, businessman Dick Smith, and billionaire Gina Rinehart. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services license numbers and check regulatory records before investing, while Kohler argues that platforms hosting such content should face heavy fines.
